shots.composition_notes: Locked-off medium two-shot of the two stop-motion figures seated on a curb/step in front of a lit convenience-store entrance; both heads sit in the upper third, symmetrical left/right placement with roughly equal headroom on each; two shopping bags anchor the bottom-left corner as foreground weight; title card text ('THE ART OF REACTING') and episode label ('Episode 15') overlay the frame, meaning the actual character action is partly obscured by graphics during this shot.

Hard cut to a tighter, static medium two-shot on the same pair now framed against a dark, blurred night-street background (storefront no longer visible) -- isolates the characters from the busy store backdrop for the dialogue-heavy middle section. Woman is left-of-center holding the phone low in frame, man is right-of-center holding the ice cream cone at frame-bottom; both faces held at consistent height for the entire ~5.5s duration with no reframing, pan, or zoom detected across the periodic samples -- camera does not move once the cut lands.

Cuts back to the original storefront medium two-shot framing (same background/positions as the opening shot) but without title text, giving a clean, uncluttered view of both faces for the punchline reaction; bags and doorframe verticals reappear as framing elements; still perfectly static, no push or handheld drift.

Pure graphic end card on solid black: series title centered in the upper-middle third, 'Created by Nin.' subtitle beneath it, and a small ribbon-style 'NEW EPISODE DAILY' badge lower-center -- no camera or characters, static text/graphic layout only.

framing_patterns_notes: The video relies entirely on static locked-off shots and hard cuts rather than any pans, tilts, zooms, or handheld movement -- every camera change in this reel is a cut, not an in-shot move. It also reuses the exact same medium two-shot composition (character positions, eyeline height, phone/ice-cream props in the same hands) for both the cold-open/title shot and the punchline shot, book-ending the tighter reaction shot in between; this bookend framing lets the punchline land in a visually 'familiar' shot the viewer already saw at the top, reinforcing the reveal.
